founder_intro: In 2011, Trupti Kulshreshtha established Vidya as a space where people from all walks of life could feel heard, understood and supported.
story_html:
For Trupti Kulshreshtha, psychology has never been just a profession. It has been a journey of understanding people, their struggles, their strengths, and the many different ways in which people experience life.

Over the course of her career, Trupti has had the opportunity to work with several NGOs and organisations, closely supporting people from vulnerable and challenging backgrounds. Her work brought her in contact with children and adolescents in crisis, children in conflict with the law, girls facing difficult circumstances, survivors of trauma and trafficking, and individuals dealing with complex emotional and social challenges.

These experiences gave Trupti a deep and meaningful understanding of human behaviour and resilience. Working closely with people who were going through some of the most difficult phases of their lives gave her immense professional satisfaction. She experienced firsthand how being heard, understood and supported could make a difference in someone's life.

But while working with vulnerable communities, Trupti began noticing another reality around her.

She could see that mental health concerns were not limited to the people she was professionally working with. They were present all around her—in families, schools, workplaces and relationships.

Students were struggling with academic pressure and anxiety. Parents were overwhelmed by responsibilities. Couples were facing relationship difficulties. Working professionals were experiencing stress and emotional exhaustion. Many people were dealing with loneliness, grief, confusion and a loss of direction.

Yet, unlike many visible physical or social problems, these struggles were often difficult to notice.

People could appear completely fine on the outside while experiencing significant emotional difficulties within. Their problems were not always recognised by society, and sometimes they were not even recognised by the individuals themselves.

This created a growing restlessness within Trupti.

On one side, she was experiencing immense satisfaction through her NGO work and the opportunity to support vulnerable communities. On the other, she found herself deeply concerned about the psychological struggles she was witnessing among the general public.

She began to feel that there was a need for a space where people could seek psychological support before their difficulties became overwhelming—a space where a person did not need to prove that their problem was “serious enough” to ask for help.

This restlessness eventually became the inspiration for Vidya Counseling Centre, which Trupti established in 2011.

Vidya Counseling Centre became an extension of everything she had learned through her years of work. It gave her the opportunity to bring her experience of working with vulnerable populations into a space that was open to people from all walks of life.

The story behind “Vidya”

The name Vidya has a deeply personal meaning for Trupti.

Vidya was her mother's name.

Although her mother is no longer with her, Trupti continues to carry a deep sense of gratitude towards her. Her mother's presence, values and influence remain an important part of Trupti's personal journey.

Choosing the name Vidya Counseling Centre was therefore not simply a professional decision. It was Trupti's way of expressing her gratitude and keeping her mother's name connected to something that is deeply meaningful to her.

Today, Vidya represents more than a counseling centre.

It represents Trupti's journey—from working closely with vulnerable communities, to recognising the quieter and less visible mental health struggles within society, and finally creating a space where people from all backgrounds can seek understanding and support.

What began with a sense of restlessness became a purpose.

And that purpose continues to guide Trupti's work:

to create a space where people feel heard, understood and accepted—and where seeking help is seen not as a weakness, but as a step towards understanding oneself and living a healthier, more fulfilling life.
